extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of classical rhetoric, orators, legal advocates, and anyone studying rhetorical humor and decorum
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance from Quintilian (Institutio Oratoria VI.3) on producing and judging wit in forensic and conversational oratory, emphasizing urbanitas, decorum (aptum), and specific techniques and prohibitions. Intended to help an orator choose apt, effective, and non-damaging humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three sources of laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter is derived from one of three places: (1) the physical appearance of one's opponent (face, gesture, dress); (2) his character as revealed in his words and actions; (3) external sources (circumstances, accident, surroundings). All forms of raillery reduce to one of these heads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing or diagnosing a joke, determine which of the three sources it springs from; this taxonomy captures the universe of effective raillery and helps tailor the material to target (appearance, character, or situation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Categorization of sayings: severa / hilara / media
rubrics_metrics.description: Sayings (dicta) are classified as: Severa (serious), Hilara (humorous), Media (intermediate) — the ones blending both registers, often the most useful for the orator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer media (mixed-register) remarks for oratory because they balance seriousness and humour; choose register according to case and audience so the remark supports rather than undermines the speaker's purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Urbanitas (city-tinctured, learned style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Urbanitas denotes 'language with a smack of the city in its words, accent and idiom' plus a 'tincture of learning derived from associating with well-educated men.' It is the opposite of rusticitas (provincial coarseness) and marks one who can speak with humour and appropriateness in any setting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate urbane language and learned touches without sliding into affectation; urbanitas signals wit combined with education and social polish, making humour acceptable and effective in refined contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aptum — appropriateness to audience, occasion, and speaker
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour must always be governed by aptum — the right joke to the right audience at the right moment, and fit the speaker's standing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before using wit, assess audience sensibilities, the occasion's gravity, and your own social/legal position. Aptum is the controlling norm: even clever material is wrong if mismatched to situation or speaker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve dignity; avoid buffoonery
rubrics_metrics.description: The orator never sacrifices dignity for a laugh. Avoid jokes aimed at deep misfortune (pity defeats laughter), deep crime (indignation defeats laughter), anything the audience will deem cruel, or any joke that makes the orator unintentionally ridiculous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: trading dignity for cheap laughs, mocking victims of misfortune, punching up at crimes that provoke indignation, or staging stunts that leave the speaker humiliated. The aim is to look like a witty orator, not a buffoon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger zones where wit can ruin a case
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit can be damaging if directed at: one's own client; powerful judges or persons present; things sacred or universally revered; misfortunes the audience pities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these targets as off-limits or approach with extreme caution. Even a well-crafted jest may backfire in these zones by alienating decision-makers or invoking pity/indignation that harms the speaker's cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approved rhetorical techniques for wit
rubrics_metrics.description: Quintilian catalogs techniques: saying something contrary to expectation (inopinatum), reproof under the guise of praise or vice versa, pretending not to understand (dissimulatio), quoting an opponent's words back altered, applying proverbs to new situations, controlled ambiguity, mocking comparison (to a worse exemplar), etymological play, and self-deprecation when it shows confidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these devices with judgment and moderation (ambiguity 'sparingly'); deploy techniques that suit the target source of laughter and maintain aptum and dignity. Self-deprecation is permitted only insofar as it signals confidence rather than weakness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic checklist for evaluating a joke
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions to test a proposed jest: Does the joke arise from one of the three sources (appearance, character, external)? Is it apt to audience, occasion, and speaker's standing? Does dignity survive? Does the orator look like a wit, not a buffoon? Does the joke risk evoking pity or indignation that would defeat it?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this checklist before speaking: if any answer is negative (e.g., risks pity/indignation, undermines dignity, mismatches audience), revise or discard the jest. Use the questions as a pre-deployment safety filter.
